In plain words

Ivanti released fixes for two more security problems in its Connect Secure remote-access product, which attackers had combined with an earlier flaw to take full control of affected systems without logging in. The attacks have been active since at least October and could affect organizations that expose these Ivanti systems to the internet; more than 5,000 such systems are currently visible online. These systems can provide a direct path into company networks, putting sensitive business and customer information at risk, so organizations using them need to install the updates quickly.

Summary
Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure flaws, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527, that attackers chained with the previously patched CVE-2026-104935 authentication bypass to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. Administrators should urgently update exposed Connect Secure gateways, as exploitation has been active since early October.

Ivanti released security updates for two additional Connect Secure flaws, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527, that have been used in chained zero-day attacks since at least October 1. CVE-2026-111357 is a high-severity flaw that can let an attacker gain greater control, while CVE-2026-118527 allows authenticated attackers to upload files to an unpatched device. The two flaws were used alongside CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass Ivanti patched in October.

Volexity reported that UTA0576 chained the three flaws to gain root-level code execution without authentication on fully patched Connect Secure devices. The actor reportedly did not install malware or a web shell, instead re-exploiting the device for each command and tampering with logs to evade Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool. CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and directed U.S. federal agencies to patch by Friday, while Shadowserver tracks more than 5,000 internet-exposed Connect Secure instances.

  • The attackers avoided installing malware or a web shell, instead reusing the security flaws for every command and altering logs to evade Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool.
  • Ivanti initially prioritized fixing CVE-2026-104935 because it addressed the primary attack path, while the related privilege-escalation flaw was identified during that response.
  • More than 5,000 Ivanti Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet, and the article says it is unknown how many have been secured against the ongoing attacks.
  • CISA added the earlier CVE-2026-104935 flaw to its actively exploited vulnerabilities catalog and required U.S. federal agencies to patch by Friday.
Key Points

  • 02CVE-2026-111357 is a high-severity privilege-escalation flaw, while CVE-2026-118527 allows authenticated attackers to upload files to unpatched devices.
  • 03Attackers combined these flaws with the previously patched CVE-2026-104935 authentication bypass to gain unauthenticated root-level code execution on fully patched Connect Secure devices.
  • 04Volexity reported that the UTA0576 threat actor repeatedly re-exploited affected devices for each command and altered logs rather than deploying malware or a web shell.
  • 05CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch by Friday.

In plain words

More than 1,000 GitLab servers connected to the internet have not been updated to fix a critical flaw that criminals are already using. The flaw can let an outsider run their own commands on an affected server without needing an account, using a specially designed entry in a project’s automated build settings. Organizations that run their own GitLab systems, including a platform used by more than half of Fortune 100 companies, could have code, credentials, and other sensitive information put at risk unless they install the available updates.

Summary
More than 1,000 internet-exposed GitLab servers remain unpatched against CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that attackers are actively exploiting. Administrators should immediately upgrade self-managed GitLab CE or EE instances to versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, 19.2.8, or later.

More than 1,000 internet-exposed GitLab servers remain unpatched against CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity flaw that attackers are actively exploiting for remote code execution. The issue is an integer overflow in GitLab’s CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, where a specially crafted regular expression in a pipeline configuration can allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code on a GitLab server. GitLab issued fixes on October 12 for Community and Enterprise Edition versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8, and urged self-managed customers to upgrade immediately.

CISA confirmed exploitation in the wild, added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. GitLab.com is already patched, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action, leaving self-managed deployments as the primary systems requiring updates. Shadowserver also reported more than 11,300 instances vulnerable to another maximum-severity GitLab code-execution flaw, CVE-2026-110264, out of roughly 39,000 GitLab instances it sees daily.

  • Despite patches being available for three weeks, Shadowserver still observed more than 1,000 internet-exposed GitLab instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-97229 while attacks were ongoing.
  • The exposure is broader than the newly exploited flaw alone: Shadowserver reported over 11,300 instances vulnerable to the separate maximum-severity CVE-2026-110264, from about 39,000 GitLab instances it sees daily.
  • GitLab.com was already running a patched release and GitLab Dedicated customers did not need to act, so the urgent remediation burden falls on organizations operating self-managed GitLab installations.
  • CISA has added six GitLab vulnerabilities to its actively exploited catalog since November 2021, including one that was used in ransomware attacks.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-97229 is a maximum-severity GitLab flaw in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution through a specially crafted regular expression in a pipeline configuration.
  • 02GitLab released fixes for self-managed Community and Enterprise Edition installations in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8, while GitLab.com is already patched.
  • 03CISA confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 and added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, directing U.S. federal agencies to secure affected servers by Sunday.
  • 04Shadowserver reported that it tracks more than 1,000 internet-exposed GitLab instances still vulnerable to CVE-2026-97229.
  • 05Shadowserver also reported more than 11,300 GitLab instances vulnerable to the separate maximum-severity CVE-2026-110264 flaw, out of roughly 39,000 GitLab instances it observes daily.

In plain words

The article describes a serious flaw in many versions of Linux, the software that runs servers and the computers behind many online services. An outsider could potentially use it to take full control of an internet-reachable server without needing an account, especially where a certain connection feature is enabled. This affects the underlying machines used by cloud services and containers, so updating the server software and restarting those machines is urgent even when a website sits behind a proxy or load balancer.

Summary
CVE-2026-98432 is a critical Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free flaw that may enable unauthenticated remote code execution on reachable MPTCP-enabled services. Install your vendor’s patched kernel and reboot immediately; disabling MPTCP and filtering IPv4 IP options are only temporary mitigations.

CVE-2026-98432 is a critical flaw in Linux kernel IPv4 TCP connection handling that affects kernel 4.4 and later. The Linux kernel CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10, while vendor assessments vary because the issue relies on winning a timing race. Anthropic reported that an unreleased Claude research model produced an exploit that gained root-level command execution on a Linux server with an MPTCP listener. No vendor advisory had reported exploitation in the wild as of October 29, 2026.

The flaw occurs when the kernel can free connection-related IP-options memory while another processor is still using it, potentially allowing memory disclosure, memory corruption, or a crash. Internet-reachable Linux hosts with IPv4 TCP ports are affected, including cloud virtual machines and the underlying nodes that run containers; a proxy on the same host does not prevent the kernel from handling the connection. The complete remediation is to install the vendor-patched kernel and reboot into it, while disabling MPTCP or dropping IPv4 packets carrying IP options are temporary measures. Operators should verify the running kernel with uname -r, because installing an update without rebooting does not activate the fix.

  • Go 1.24 and later programs request MPTCP listeners by default where the kernel permits it, which can expose a Go server even if its operator did not intentionally enable that feature.
  • A proxy running on the same Linux host does not protect that host, because its kernel still processes the incoming TCP connection before the proxy handles application traffic.
  • An installed kernel update is not sufficient until the machine restarts into it; the article notes that a host may appear fixed in scanning results even though it is still running the old kernel.
  • According to Anthropic, a failed attempt at the timing-dependent exploit only fails that connection attempt rather than crashing the target, allowing an attacker to keep retrying.
  • For containers, the relevant software to patch is the Linux kernel on the underlying node, not the container image itself.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-98432 is a Linux kernel IPv4 TCP use-after-free flaw affecting kernel version 4.4 and later, which the kernel CVE team rates 9.8 out of 10.
  • 02Anthropic reported that an unreleased Claude research model produced an exploit that achieved root-level command execution on a Linux server with an MPTCP listener.
  • 03Installing a vendor-patched kernel and rebooting is the complete remediation, while disabling MPTCP or dropping IPv4 packets with IP options are temporary exposure-reduction measures.
  • 04Internet-reachable Linux hosts, including EC2 instances, ECS container instances, and EKS nodes, are affected when they expose an IPv4 TCP port; the container host kernel is what matters for containers.
  • 05No vendor advisory had reported exploitation in the wild as of October 29, 2026.

In plain words

Synology says criminals are breaking into older versions of the software used by its network storage devices and locking owners’ files so they can demand payment. The people most at risk are Synology device owners who have not installed updates, especially if their device’s settings page can be reached from the internet. This matters because these devices often hold important personal or business data, and the company tracks more than 380,000 that are exposed online. Owners should update the device software, turn on automatic updates, and remove public access to its management page.

Summary
Synology warns that C3RB3R ransomware operators are exploiting a December 2024-patched DSM vulnerability to encrypt data on outdated Internet-exposed NAS devices. Users should immediately update DSM, enable automatic updates, and block public access to the NAS management interface.

Synology has warned that threat actors are using a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to deploy C3RB3R ransomware against NAS devices running outdated DiskStation Manager (DSM) versions. The attacks encrypt victims’ data and demand payment for a purported “C3rb3r Decryptor.” Synology urged users to update DSM immediately and enable automatic updates. The company also advised blocking internet access to NAS management web interfaces.

Synology has not said which vulnerability is being exploited, but it linked to a November 2024 advisory covering CVE-2024-10441, CVE-2024-50629, and CVE-2024-10445. Those flaws could allow an attacker to execute code, read files, or write files on unpatched devices. Affected users reported that encrypted files receive a .L0CK3D extension and that the malware leaves a read-me3.txt ransom note. The note warns against using third-party recovery software and directs victims to a dark-web payment portal.

The warning follows more than two weeks of user reports and is unusual for Synology, whose prior comparable warning was published in August 2019. Shadowserver tracks more than 380,000 Synology NAS devices exposed to the internet, although it does not show how many are protected against the attacks. The current C3RB3R operation uses the name of the older Cerber ransomware service and has previously been used against Atlassian Confluence and GitLab servers.

  • The ransomware campaign targets a flaw that Synology patched in December 2024, showing that devices left on older DSM releases remain exposed long after fixes are available.
  • Synology rarely issues alerts about active attacks against its customers; its previous comparable warning was in August 2019, following brute-force activity associated with eCh0raix ransomware infections.
  • Affected users can recognize this campaign through the .L0CK3D extension and the read-me3.txt ransom note advertising a “C3rb3r Decryptor.”
  • The article identifies internet exposure of the NAS management interface as a preventable risk factor, alongside installing the specified DSM updates and enabling automatic updates.
  • The current C3RB3R operation shares its name with the older Cerber ransomware service but is described as a separate operation that has also targeted Confluence and GitLab servers since December 2021.
Key Points
  • 01Synology warned that C3RB3R ransomware actors are exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to target NAS devices running outdated DiskStation Manager software.
  • 02The attacks encrypt data and demand payment for a purported "C3rb3r Decryptor," with affected users reporting a read-me3.txt ransom note and a .L0CK3D file extension.
  • 03Synology advised users to update DSM immediately, enable automatic updates, and block internet access to the management web interface.
  • 04Synology linked the active attacks to a November 2024 advisory covering CVE-2024-10441, CVE-2024-50629, and CVE-2024-10445, though it did not identify which specific flaw is being exploited.
  • 05Shadowserver tracks more than 380,000 internet-exposed Synology NAS devices, although it does not indicate how many are patched or honeypots.

In plain words

A Chinese hacking group called Vapor Panda used an AI-powered tool called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations in 14 countries, including government agencies, phone and internet providers, drug companies, chip makers, defense organizations, nuclear organizations, and financial firms. At least nine organizations were reportedly broken into, including phone companies in the United States and Belgium and government bodies in Greece, the Middle East, and Latin America. The AI tool helped the attackers search for weak points, break into systems, steal login information, and try different routes quickly, while human operators stepped in for key decisions. This matters because it shows that one group can use AI to run many large-scale break-in attempts at once.

Summary
Chinese-linked Vapor Panda used the ARTEX AI multi-agent penetration-testing framework to automate cyberespionage against more than 200 organizations in 14 countries, compromising at least nine. The campaign demonstrates how human-directed AI agents can scale reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft, and lateral movement across multiple targets simultaneously.

Chinese-linked threat actor Vapor Panda used ARTEX AI, a multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in a cyberespionage campaign targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The operation began on October 17 and targeted government ministries, telecommunications providers, and organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors. CrowdStrike reported that at least nine organizations were compromised, while password-spraying and credential-scanning activity affected at least 12 additional high-value targets.

CrowdStrike said the attackers used DeepSeek and an unidentified commercial language model to coordinate planning and worker agents across simultaneous intrusions, with human operators intervening for critical decisions. The agents conducted reconnaissance, exploited vulnerabilities, deployed web shells, obtained credentials, and sought alternative attack paths; operators also instructed them to avoid Windows hosts protected by CrowdStrike Falcon. Separately, DIVD said ARTEX AI autonomously gained root privileges in its September 2026 breach within 12 minutes by chaining a Zammad zero-day with a second local privilege-escalation zero-day, generating more than 450,000 requests and 2,500 scripts.

  • The operators directed AI agents in Chinese but personally intervened at critical decision points, indicating that the campaign combined automated execution with human oversight rather than relying entirely on autonomous activity.
  • The attackers explicitly told the agents to avoid Windows systems protected by CrowdStrike Falcon and instead focus on hosts without that protection.
  • CrowdStrike estimated that AI agents used more than 1.4 billion input tokens during one intrusion, illustrating the unusually large volume of automated activity involved.
  • DIVD recorded more than 450,000 requests and 2,500 scripts during its ARTEX AI incident and characterized the activity as highly noisy and disorganized.
Key Points
  • 01CrowdStrike says the China-linked threat actor Vapor Panda used the ARTEX AI penetration-testing framework in a campaign targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries beginning October 17.
  • 02The campaign targeted government ministries, telecommunications providers, and organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors, and compromised at least nine organizations.
  • 03Vapor Panda used DeepSeek and an unidentified commercial language model to coordinate AI agents that conducted reconnaissance, exploited flaws, deployed web shells, collected credentials, and pursued alternative paths during multiple intrusions.
  • 04In an intrusion against a Greek government entity, researchers say the agents forged an administrator token and read mailboxes using authentication keys from a 2022 mail-server directory export.
  • 05The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure said ARTEX AI autonomously gained root privileges on its network in 12 minutes by chaining a Zammad zero-day with a second zero-day for local privilege escalation.

    In plain words

    Google shut down parts of a network that controlled more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV streaming boxes, after finding that manufacturer Videostrong likely built in a hidden way for criminals to take control of them. The devices could be used without owners knowing to fake online ad views, route strangers’ internet traffic through home connections, and collect information from the boxes. Since the hidden software is built into the device’s core system and can return after a restart, many owners may need the maker’s help or a replacement device, while businesses must also consider risky home smart devices connected near work systems.

    Summary
    Google disrupted a 1.3 million-device Android botnet tied to Videostrong, which it says deliberately embedded the x.cpe backdoor in TV boxes and sold criminal access. Because the backdoor is firmware-level and survives normal cleanup, affected owners may need vendor remediation or device replacement.

    Google led a late-October operation that disrupted a botnet controlling more than 1.3 million Android devices, mainly TV set-top boxes. Google said it is highly confident that Shenzhen-based device maker Videostrong intentionally included the x.cpe backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminals. The company has banned Videostrong and future affiliates from building or selling certified Android devices and from supplying software to certified device makers.

    The firmware-level x.cpe backdoor ran with system access, contacted control servers for instructions, and could disable Google Play Protect before silently installing software. Operators used it to collect device and account information, take screenshots, run remote commands, and turn devices into residential proxies or tools for ad-view fraud. Because the backdoor reinstalls after a restart, affected owners cannot reliably remove it themselves; TrendAI said remediation requires vendor action, platform protection, or replacement, while Synthient advised organizations to identify, disconnect, and discard affected devices.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, which the company says consisted of more than 1.3 million Android TV streaming boxes manufactured by Chinese company Videostrong Technology Co. Google assessed with high confidence that Videostrong intentionally embedded a persistent backdoor into device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates. Google revoked Videostrong’s Android TV license and banned the company and its future affiliates from producing certified Android devices or supplying software to certified vendors.

The XCPE backdoor, tracked as x.cpe and com.oemservice, operated with Android system-level privileges and contacted command-and-control infrastructure to receive instructions. Operators could install apps, disable Google Play Protect, run commands, capture screenshots, inject keystrokes, collect device and account data, and establish remote access. Google said the devices were also used for ad fraud and residential proxy services, while the disrupted infrastructure served more than a dozen related malware families and affected at least 10 million additional compromised devices. Although the command infrastructure was disrupted, the malware remains on affected devices and can reinstall itself from the /oem/ partition unless users install clean firmware or disconnect the devices from the internet.

In plain words

Security researchers found serious weaknesses in Langflow, a tool used to build AI assistants and automated workflows. In affected versions, someone on the internet may be able to get around the login screen or make the server run commands without having an account. This puts organizations using Langflow at risk of outsiders taking control of systems or accessing sensitive information, so they should update to version 1.13.0.

Summary
Langflow versions 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 contain critical flaws that can let unauthenticated attackers bypass authentication and execute code remotely, including through MCP tool enumeration. Organizations should upgrade to Langflow 1.13.0 immediately, as IBM provides no workaround.

IBM reported four Langflow vulnerabilities affecting every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8, including two critical issues rated 9.8. CVE-2026-93680 can let an unauthenticated attacker bypass authentication, while CVE-2026-110186 can allow unauthenticated remote code execution through Model Context Protocol tool enumeration. The other issues could allow a low-privileged user to cause operating-system commands to run on the server or obtain sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials.

A public Metasploit Framework module already connects to vulnerable Langflow MCP endpoints without credentials, opens a session, and lists available tools, though it does not execute commands. Langflow’s automatic-login setting was enabled by default in version 1.12.8 and can log users in as superusers; version 1.13.0 turns it off by default. Version 1.13.0, released on October 22, is the only stated fix for these four issues, and IBM offers no workaround for organizations unable to upgrade.

  • Version 1.12.8 was released on the same day as 1.13.0 but still contains the critical flaws, making an upgrade specifically to 1.13.0 necessary rather than simply moving to the latest 1.12 release.
  • Automatic login was enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8 and logs users in as superusers; IBM’s bulletin does not clarify whether servers with that setting disabled remain vulnerable.
  • A public Metasploit module already supports unauthenticated access to Langflow’s MCP endpoint for CVE-2026-93680, although the module itself only starts a session and enumerates available tools rather than executing commands.
  • Organizations upgrading from automatic login need to prepare existing accounts for password sign-in, and Langflow warns that deleting or reinstalling the product to recover access can permanently remove saved flows.

  • 03A public Metasploit Framework module for CVE-2026-93680 can connect to Langflow's MCP endpoint without credentials, start a session, and list available tools.

  • 05Langflow 1.13.0 disables automatic login by default; the setting was enabled by default in version 1.12.8 and can log users in as superusers without prompting for sign-in.

In plain words

Researchers found a spying campaign aimed at Linux computers used by government bodies and government-linked organizations. The attackers used a program called SysGoRAT, hidden access points, and password-stealing tricks to stay in systems, search email, and try to take sensitive information. Some of their scripts appear to have been produced with AI, suggesting that AI can help attackers create and adapt harmful tools more quickly, putting public-sector information and accounts at greater risk.

Summary
Palo Alto Networks uncovered CL-UNK-1211, an espionage campaign targeting government-linked Linux servers with the SysGoRAT backdoor, web shells, credential theft, mailbox collection, and persistence mechanisms. Researchers say scripts with conversational reasoning notes may indicate attackers used AI tools or autonomous agents to rapidly generate and deploy post-exploitation code.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported that a cyber-espionage cluster tracked as CL-UNK-1211 targeted Linux infrastructure linked to government entities and state-affiliated organizations between October 2025 and April 2026. The operators conducted reconnaissance, sought to maintain long-term access, attempted to dump sensitive databases, and targeted government mailboxes in an effort to access social-media accounts. Unit 42 said the campaign combined open-source tools, custom backdoors, and web shells, while also attempting to disable endpoint protections, erase logs, and leave deceptive red-team markers.

The attackers used malicious PHP and shell scripts for persistence, reconnaissance, credential collection, and data theft, with several scripts containing conversational explanations of their logic. Unit 42 said these notes suggest the scripts may have been copied from an AI prompt response or deployed by an automated AI agent. The campaign also used SysGoRAT, a custom Go-based remote-access trojan for Windows and Linux that connects to a hard-coded command-and-control address and can execute commands, provide interactive shells, transfer files, establish persistence, and relay network traffic.

Credential theft methods included replacing .bashrc with a malicious version, adding password-harvesting code to PHP login pages, and searching configuration files and command history for cleartext credentials. The attackers also searched mail directories and deployed a PHP script to identify social-media-related emails, although a separate script intended to compress collected mail failed because of syntax errors. Unit 42 described the activity as an example of attackers combining conventional post-compromise methods with AI-accelerated workflows to increase operational speed while reducing manual development work.

  • Conversational, step-by-step reasoning embedded in malicious scripts gave Unit 42 a potential indicator that the code was copied directly from an AI response or deployed through an automated AI agent.
  • The attackers paired credential theft with targeted mailbox searches for social-media-related messages, indicating that email content and associated account access were both collection priorities.
  • SysGoRAT’s ability to run on Linux and Windows, establish interactive shells, transfer files, and relay traffic through arbitrary TCP connections gave the operators a single backdoor with multiple ways to maintain and extend access.
  • The attackers tried to make their activity resemble an authorized security assessment by planting deceptive red-team markers while also disabling protections and deleting logs, which could complicate incident investigation.
  • AI-assisted tooling did not eliminate operational mistakes: the attempted zip_mails.sh email-collection script contained syntax errors and failed to run.

  • 03The campaign used a custom Go-based remote-access trojan called SysGoRAT, which connects over WebSocket to a hard-coded command-and-control address and works on both Linux and Windows.
  • 04The attackers sought credentials by replacing .bashrc files, inserting credential-harvesting code into PHP login pages, and searching configuration and command-history files for cleartext passwords.

In plain words

Kaspersky found attacks on education organizations in several countries in Africa and Latin America that used CyberStrikeAI, a publicly available tool that lets an AI system help direct a hacker’s actions on infected computers. A person still chose the overall goal, but the AI helped decide which familiar steps to take, such as looking through networks, stealing account information, moving between computers, and collecting database data. This matters because AI can make serious break-ins faster and easier for less-skilled attackers, even though the harmful actions themselves are already known and can still be detected.

Summary
Kaspersky identified attacks against education-sector organizations in Africa and Latin America using the open-source CyberStrikeAI framework, where a server-side LLM orchestrated post-exploitation actions through conventional C2 implants. The AI did not introduce novel host-side techniques, but accelerated familiar domain-compromise activity including reconnaissance, credential dumping, lateral movement, and database collection.

Kaspersky’s Cyber Threat Intelligence team identified a campaign against education-sector organizations in several countries in Africa and Latin America that used the open-source CyberStrikeAI framework. Attackers initially accessed a compromised Microsoft SQL Server manually, then deployed a CyberStrikeAI agent to conduct persistence, reconnaissance, lateral movement, credential theft, and database collection. The framework’s server-side LLM orchestrator selected tools and generated commands, while the implant on compromised hosts executed those commands.

The article describes how attackers used scheduled tasks, PowerShell, WMI, SMB shares, Impacket, Mimikatz, registry-hive dumping, LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, and Golden Ticket attacks to compromise privileged domain accounts. In one incident, the operation progressed from agent deployment to domain administrator compromise within roughly three to four days, with some lateral movement, credential dumping, and database export activity completed in about an hour. Kaspersky emphasizes that the AI component did not create fundamentally new on-host behavior: defenders can detect the campaign through established endpoint and network monitoring for familiar post-exploitation techniques and CyberStrikeAI command-and-control patterns.

  • The AI component was not installed inside victim networks: it ran on the attackers’ command-and-control server, so affected computers showed ordinary remote-control behavior rather than local AI-service requests or unusual AI-related resource use.
  • CyberStrikeAI’s self-signed TLS certificate is recreated whenever its control panel starts, making the certificate’s not-before timestamp useful for reconstructing server restart chronology from scans.
  • The implant’s fixed X-Implant-Token HTTP header is embedded during payload creation and can link samples to the same command-and-control server as both a network and malware indicator.
  • Because Windows and Linux implants in each sample group shared identical Go build metadata, analysts could establish that they were built from the same project working copy; however, separate infrastructure and server versions prevented linking the two groups to one operator.
  • The article notes that AI-generated commands can vary between executions and reduce operator-specific behavioral signatures, which makes traditional behavior-based attribution less reliable even though detection of the underlying techniques remains feasible.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky identified a campaign targeting education-sector organizations in several African and Latin American countries that used the open-source CyberStrikeAI framework during post-exploitation.
  • 02CyberStrikeAI keeps its LLM-based decision-making on the command-and-control server, while its implant on compromised machines polls for tasks and executes commands without AI functionality of its own.
  • 03In one reconstructed incident, attackers moved from agent deployment to compromising domain administrator accounts in roughly three to four days, using reconnaissance, persistence, credential dumping, lateral movement, and database export.
  • 04Observed credential-access activity included registry-hive dumping, LSASS process dumping through comsvcs.dll MiniDump, and DCSync and Golden Ticket attacks using a renamed Mimikatz utility.
  • 05The article states that established endpoint and network detections can identify the observed behavior because the AI-directed implant performed familiar post-exploitation techniques rather than fundamentally new host-side actions.

In plain words

An Iran-linked spying group called DarkBlinders used convincing fake job offers, fake cloud-service websites, and counterfeit software to gain access to a prominent person in Israel and a Kurdish regional government cloud environment in Iraq. The group’s harmful programs let it remotely control infected computers, steal information, and maintain access over time. This matters because the campaign shows how carefully tailored scams can reach government-related and high-value targets, potentially exposing sensitive information and services.

Summary
Iran-aligned DarkBlinders used tailored phishing, fake recruitment coding tests, and counterfeit software to compromise an Israeli target and an Iraqi Kurdish government cloud environment, deploying ShelbyLoader/ShelbyC2 and Blackwood. Researchers assess the activity may be linked to broader Iran-nexus clusters associated with APT34.

Dream Research Labs reported that Iran-aligned DarkBlinders compromised a high-profile individual in Israel and additional targets in a government cloud environment in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region between August and October 2026. The group, active since at least September 2024, has previously targeted aviation and telecommunications organizations in the United Arab Emirates and Iraq. Researchers said the campaign combines credential phishing with malware delivery through government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains. The activity underscores DarkBlinders’ continued focus on tailored social engineering against high-value and government-related targets.

DarkBlinders used fake recruitment outreach, malicious Visual Studio coding assessments, and a counterfeit videoconferencing application named StarkMeet to deliver its tools. Its attack chain used a malicious C# project file, AppDomainManager injection, and DLL sideloading to run ShelbyLoader V2, which then launched the ShelbyC2 backdoor and deployed the Blackwood tunneling utility. ShelbyC2 has been associated with GitHub-based command-and-control, data exfiltration, and remote control. Dream assessed with medium confidence that DarkBlinders overlaps with UNC5795 and Dust Specter, and that related clusters may be operationally connected to the broader APT34 group.

  • The fake recruitment application was designed to appear harmless at first: submitting its questionnaire did not send data anywhere, helping build trust before the victim received the malicious coding assessment.
  • DarkBlinders combined credential-theft websites with malware delivery, using lookalike government, webmail, and cloud-service domains rather than relying on a single delivery method.
  • The group used developer-oriented materials, including a Visual Studio project presented as a coding test, to target high-value job seekers while disguising malicious software as routine professional work.
  • Researchers linked DarkBlinders to other Iran-nexus activity through shared infrastructure, victim targeting, and malware evidence, but characterized the broader APT34 connection as only medium confidence.
  • Separately, the Iranian-linked Prince of Persia group operated a command server in the United States in 2026, an unusual location for the group after a three-month period of inactivity.

In plain words

Attackers pretended to be company IT support staff in Microsoft Teams and convinced employees to let them control their computers through Windows’ Quick Assist tool. They then took advantage of unsafe company login settings to impersonate powerful internal accounts, access key systems, and in one case copy company files to an outside server. This matters because changing passwords or wiping a computer may not remove that access, so organizations need to verify unexpected support requests and secure the systems that issue employee login credentials.

Summary
Attackers impersonated IT support on Microsoft Teams to gain remote access through Quick Assist, then abused insecure Active Directory Certificate Services configurations to obtain privileged certificates, access domain controllers, and exfiltrate data. Organizations should harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8, restrict external Teams contact and remote-support tools, and ensure no privileged identities are excluded from containment.

Microsoft investigated two intrusions in which attackers posed as internal IT support through Microsoft Teams and persuaded employees to provide Quick Assist connection codes. The attackers then gained hands-on control of employee workstations and used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts. Microsoft said one incident resulted in company data being copied to an external server, and it did not attribute the activity to a known group.

In the first case, attackers abused an ESC1 certificate template to impersonate privileged accounts, accessed a domain controller, began DCSync activity, and used a renamed Rclone tool to copy files to an external SFTP server. In the second, they used PetitPotam to coerce a domain controller authentication and relayed it to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint, an ESC8 technique, to obtain a certificate for the domain controller; isolating the compromised workstation stopped further activity. Microsoft recommended verifying unexpected support requests, restricting external Teams contact and remote-support tools, securing AD CS templates and enrollment endpoints, auditing certificate activity, and ensuring that any account excluded from automatic containment receives a manual response.

  • A certificate obtained through a weak Active Directory Certificate Services template can remain usable even after the associated account password is reset or the originally compromised computer is wiped.
  • Containing most compromised privileged accounts was insufficient in the first case because one excluded account remained usable and enabled continued access and data theft.
  • The attackers signed in to a domain controller and began copying Active Directory password data within seconds of obtaining a certificate, showing how little time defenders may have after certificate abuse is detected.
  • Revoking a maliciously issued certificate does not invalidate Kerberos tickets that were already issued, so organizations must also review active tickets during response.
  • Windows Server 2025 enables Extended Protection for Authentication by default for Active Directory Certificate Services, while Windows Server 2019 and 2022 require it to be enabled manually.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers impersonated internal IT or help-desk staff through Microsoft Teams and persuaded employees to provide Quick Assist connection codes, giving them remote control of workstations.
  • 02Microsoft investigated two intrusions in which attackers abused insecure Active Directory Certificate Services configurations to obtain certificates for privileged accounts or a domain controller.
  • 03In the first intrusion, attackers exploited an ESC1 certificate template, performed DCSync on a domain controller, and used a renamed Rclone utility to transfer company data from a file share to an external SFTP server.
  • 04In the second intrusion, attackers used PetitPotam and NTLM relay against an AD CS web enrollment endpoint to obtain a domain-controller certificate, but workstation isolation stopped further activity.
  • 05Microsoft recommends restricting external Teams contact and remote-support tools, reviewing certificate-template permissions, enabling HTTPS and Extended Protection for Authentication on enrollment endpoints, and auditing certificate issuance.

Summary
Hackers compromised Ukraine’s Air Alert app and Russia’s EMERCOM app to send fabricated nuclear, radiation, and attack warnings, though both countries said their primary emergency alert infrastructure remained unaffected.

Ukraine’s Air Alert app, used by millions for missile, drone, and other emergency warnings, was apparently compromised on Sunday and sent Kyiv residents fake notifications about radiation hazards, chemical threats, street fighting, and a possible Oreshnik missile strike. The Ukrainian Air Force said the app had likely been compromised by the enemy and told residents to disregard the messages. One Russian-language alert included a link to a Telegram channel associated with a previously unknown group calling itself Hitcore Corp, which claimed responsibility.

The app’s developers disabled push notifications and temporarily suspended service before gradually restoring basic alerts by early Monday, while keeping the threat map disabled and adding security measures. Ukrainian authorities said the national warning system and Kyiv’s separate Kyiv Digital app continued to work normally, and developers cautioned users not to open links in suspicious notifications. Hours later, Kyiv-based group DC8044 claimed it accessed the API of Russia’s EMERCOM app and sent false nuclear-launch warnings; Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry acknowledged the app compromise but said its main warning channels, including sirens, text messages, television, and radio, were unaffected.

Cisco Talos researchers identified VOLTA-AUTODOXER, a Windows information stealer that collects browser passwords and cookies, payment-card data, cryptocurrency wallet phrases, application sessions, cloud and SSH keys, Wi-Fi profiles, and screenshots. It also assembles a structured profile of the person using the computer, including possible location and address, employer information, Slack workspaces, document metadata, and indicators of iPhone backups. VOLTA can use stolen Gmail sessions to search receipts and order histories from services such as Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal to corroborate address information.

The malware sends this evidence bundle through OpenRouter for AI analysis, using Claude Opus 4.6 by default and falling back to Kimi K2 or Gemini 2.5 Flash if a model refuses. Its AI prompt directs the model to rank a victim’s valuables by potential monetization and assess their security practices and password hygiene, turning raw stolen information into a prioritized dossier. PHP2Shell showed rapid patching by well-maintained environments while millions of older PHP deployments remain difficult or impossible to remediate without migration, backported fixes, or isolation.

PHP2Shell involved two critical memory-corruption flaws in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run code on PHP web servers under certain conditions. The bugs had existed in the codebase for more than a decade, but the article says AI helped reduce the complex research required to turn them into working exploits. Because PHP is widely used across the web, Censys observed tens of millions of Internet-facing PHP services relevant to the incident.

Censys reported that more than 11 million PHP services moved from affected to fixed versions after patches became available on October 21, with the largest patching burst occurring on October 22 and 23. However, more than 30 million services still reported affected versions as of October 29, including roughly 23 million running PHP 8.1 or older, for which no official PHP2Shell fix was available. The article argues that an organization’s ability to respond depends heavily on pre-existing visibility, ownership, vendor support, and maintenance processes, and calls for software that is easier to update, migrate, or otherwise protect when patching is not practical.

  • The article finds that the oldest exposed software is often the least likely to change: releases that were 8 to more than 20 years out of date shifted by only about a percentage point of the observed population over two and a half years.
  • Patch behavior can be driven more by established maintenance practices than by patch availability alone; Jenkins showed a steady 7.3% baseline upgrade rate, while Cleo Managed File Transfer saw a 63% spike only after reports of active exploitation.
  • For PHP2Shell, the reported PHP version did not always show whether a system was protected because vendors such as CloudLinux and Plesk backported fixes to older branches without necessarily changing the upstream version.
  • The article highlights that many PHP deployments can be patched quickly through hosting providers or downstream distributors, meaning an organization's response capability may have been determined by its software supply and support arrangements long before a critical flaw is disclosed.
  • A patch being available does not guarantee practical remediation, because older applications may require compatibility testing, coordination with providers, major migrations, or replacement or isolation of equipment that can no longer receive vendor updates.

Summary
A Brazilian DANFE phishing campaign bypassed reputation-based email controls because its call-to-action used an unresolvable, single-label hostname that received no URL verdict. The case shows that “not scanned” must be treated as risk and supplemented with URL-structure, content, and campaign-correlation analysis.

A Portuguese-language DANFE fiscal-document notice reached a senior developer at a Brazilian non-profit technology research and innovation institute. Its only call-to-action, a “Baixar DANFE” button, linked to hxxps://marxcal292e/nf/index[.]php, using a single-label hostname with no top-level domain. The URL reputation system recorded the link as “notscanned,” while Microsoft assigned the message an SCL of 1 and delivered it to the Inbox, and Vade assigned a spam score of 0.

Themis classified the email as Credential Theft at 56% confidence, and a human analyst resolved it as malicious. Structural link analysis rated the URL high risk because it had no TLD, returned NXDOMAIN, and had no WHOIS or SSL information, despite being unable to retrieve page content. About 85 minutes later, the same mailbox received a second DANFE-themed message with a new subject, showing continued campaign activity; both messages were quarantined and the second was permanently deleted.

The article argues that “not scanned,” “unknown,” and “no verdict” results should not be treated as safe outcomes. It recommends assessing URL structure independently of reputation, retaining content and language analysis when links are unscored, and correlating repeat messages to the same recipient across changing subject lines. It also notes that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC passing for a consumer freemail account confirms the sending provider, not the identity or trustworthiness of the account holder.

  • A “not scanned” URL result is an absence of information rather than evidence that a link is safe, so controls that block only positively identified malicious links can fail open.
  • Passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC did not establish that the email was legitimate, because the message was sent from an authenticated consumer freemail account and those checks only confirmed the provider sent it.
  • The link could be assessed as high risk without loading a landing page because a single-label hostname, public-DNS failure, and missing WHOIS and SSL information were anomalous for an automated invoice notice.
  • A second, reworded DANFE-themed message sent to the same recipient about 85 minutes later provided campaign evidence even though the second message body was unavailable.

  • The Hugging Face campaign did not rely on poisoned model files; it abused the trust_remote_code option so that Python code supplied with a model runs automatically when the model is loaded.

Privileged identities are user or service accounts with powerful permissions, such as administrator access.
processor concept
A processor is the main chip in a computer that runs instructions and performs calculations.
Profiling concept
Profiling is the practice of analyzing information about someone to infer their interests, behavior, or characteristics.
Prompt concept
A prompt is the instruction or question a person gives to an AI system to guide its response.
prompting technique
Prompting is the practice of giving instructions and information to an AI model to guide its response.
Prophet AI product
A security platform that uses AI agents to help investigate alerts, hunt for threats, and build detections.
Prophet AI Detection Engineer product
An AI security product that helps create, test, and improve threat-detection rules.
Prophet AI SOC Analyst product
An AI security product that investigates alerts and records its findings under configured permissions.
Prophet AI Threat Hunter product
An AI security product designed to automatically search systems for threats and detection gaps.
Prophet Security organization
Prophet Security is a cybersecurity company or product name referenced in security reporting.
Protected Health Information concept
Protected Health Information is personal medical or health-related data that is legally protected from improper use or disclosure.
proxy concept
A proxy is an intermediate server that forwards internet traffic between a user and a destination.
proxy_connect tool
A command that creates a connection through another system so traffic can be relayed to a target.
also: proxy_data, proxy_close, proxy session
Public DNS protocol
Internet-accessible Domain Name System services that translate public website names into network addresses.
public exposure threats technique
Threats to publish stolen private information in order to pressure a victim into paying or complying.
Public internet concept
The public internet is the globally accessible network that anyone can connect to through internet service providers.
public sector organization
Government organizations and publicly funded services.
Public Warning System concept
A system used by authorities to send emergency information and alerts to the public.
push notifications concept
Messages sent from an app or server to a user's device, even when the app is not actively in use.
Python tool
Python is a popular programming language often used to write scripts, automation tools, and security research code.
quarantined concept
Quarantined means a suspicious file, email, or system has been isolated so it cannot easily cause harm while it is investigated.
Quick Assist tool
Quick Assist is a Microsoft remote support tool that lets one person view or control another Windows computer with permission.
Qwen product
Qwen is a family of large language and AI models developed by Alibaba.
RAG technique
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an AI technique that looks up relevant information from external sources before generating an answer.
ransom note concept
A ransom note is a message telling a victim that files have been locked or data stolen and giving payment or contact instructions.
ransomware concept
Ransomware is malicious software or an operation that locks or steals data to pressure victims into paying money.
Ransomware Actors threat-actor
Ransomware actors are criminals who use malware to lock or steal data and demand payment from victims.
ransomware attack concept
A ransomware attack is when criminals lock files or systems and demand payment to restore access or prevent data leaks.
ransomware attacks technique
Ransomware attacks are incidents where attackers use software or methods to disrupt access and demand payment.
ransomware campaign concept
A ransomware campaign is a coordinated set of attacks where criminals encrypt or steal victims' data and demand payment.
Ransomware deployment technique
Ransomware deployment is the stage where attackers install or run ransomware on victim systems.
ransomware group threat-actor
A ransomware group is a criminal or threat-actor team that uses malware to lock or steal data and demand payment.
ransomware operators threat-actor
Ransomware operators are criminals who run attacks that lock or steal data and demand payment from victims.
Rate limits technique
Rate limits are rules that restrict how many requests a person or program can make in a set time.
rclone
Rclone is a command-line tool for syncing and copying files to cloud storage, and attackers sometimes abuse it to steal data.
Read-Only concept
A permission setting that allows someone to view information but not change it.
Readiness concept
Readiness is the state of being prepared to perform a task, job, or mission effectively.
Reasoning concept
Reasoning is the process of working through information logically to reach an answer or decision.
Reboot concept
A reboot means restarting a computer, phone, server, or other device.
reconnaissance technique
Reconnaissance is the information-gathering step attackers use to learn about a target before trying to break in.
also: systematic reconnaissance
Recover concept
Recover means restoring systems and business operations after a cyber incident.
Red Alert product
An Israeli mobile application that sends warnings about rocket attacks and other emergencies.
Red Hat organization
Red Hat is a technology company known for enterprise Linux and related software.
Red team concept
The offensive security team that simulates real-world attacks to test an organization's defenses and improve security.
Red-Team Markers technique
Clues deliberately left in an attack to make malicious activity look like an authorized security test.
also: deceptive red-team markers, legitimate security assessment
Refrigeration Systems product
Refrigeration systems are equipment that keep food or other goods cold at controlled temperatures.
regional government organization
A regional government is a public authority that administers a geographic area below the national level.
Registry concept
The Registry is a Windows database that stores system and application settings.
Registry hive concept
A registry hive is a major section of the Windows Registry that stores configuration settings for the operating system and applications.
regression concept
A regression is a new defect that makes something stop working after a change or update.
Regression testing technique
Regression testing checks that new changes did not accidentally break something that used to work.
regular expression concept
A regular expression is a special text pattern used to search for, match, or filter strings such as email addresses, file names, or suspicious commands.
relay concept
A relay is a server or service that forwards network traffic or email from one place to another.
relayed concept
Relayed means traffic or messages are passed through another system instead of going directly from sender to receiver.
remediate concept
To remediate means to fix a security problem or reduce the risk it creates.
remediation technique
Remediation is the work of fixing a security problem and reducing the damage it caused.
Remediation Guidance concept
Remediation guidance is advice on how to fix or reduce the risk from a security problem.
remote access concept
The ability to connect to another computer or network from a distant location and use it as if you were physically present.
remote access trojan malware
A remote access trojan is malware that secretly lets an attacker control a victim's computer from somewhere else.
remote commands concept
Remote commands are instructions sent over a network to make another computer or device do something.
remote control technique
Remote control means operating a computer, phone, or system from another location over a network.
Remote Desktop concept
A technology that lets you see and control a computer's desktop from another device over a network.
Remote Support product
Remote Support is software or a service that lets a technician connect to a user’s device from another location to help fix problems.
Remote Temperature Adjustments technique
Changes to a device's temperature settings made over a network rather than in person.
remote-code-execution technique
Remote code execution is a serious flaw that lets an attacker run commands on a system from elsewhere.
Remote-code-execution flaws vulnerability
Remote-code-execution flaws are vulnerabilities that can let an attacker run commands on a system from afar.
Remotely tool
Remotely is a remote administration tool that can be used to access and manage computers over a network.
Remotely Exploitable Flaw vulnerability
A security weakness that an attacker can exploit over a network without physical access to the device.
repositories concept
Repositories are places where software project files and related development data are stored.
Repository secrets concept
Repository secrets are sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, or API keys stored for use with a code repository or its automation tools.
Reputation concept
A trust score or history used by security systems to judge whether a sender, website, or file is likely safe.
Request Socket concept
A temporary Linux kernel data structure that holds connection details while a TCP connection is still being set up.
also: request socket migration
researchers organization
Researchers are people who study systems, threats, or vulnerabilities to understand and improve security.
reset their passwords technique
Reset their passwords means making users choose new passwords so old or stolen ones no longer work.
Residential proxies concept
Residential proxies route internet traffic through home-user IP addresses so it appears to come from ordinary consumers.
residential proxy tool
A residential proxy routes internet traffic through real home internet connections to make activity look like it comes from ordinary users.
residential proxy services tool
Residential proxy services route internet traffic through home-style IP addresses, which can hide the real source of activity.
Respond technique
Respond means to take action after detecting a security issue, such as containing an attack or fixing affected systems.
Restart concept
A restart is turning a device or program off and then back on again to refresh it or apply changes.
Restore technique
Restore means to bring data, settings, or a system back to an earlier working state.
Retention concept
The practice of keeping logs, records, or other data for a defined period so they can be reviewed later.
Reverse Shells technique
A remote command connection in which an infected computer calls back to an attacker's system for instructions.
also: in-memory reverse shells
review process concept
A review process is the set of steps people use to examine and approve work before it is accepted.
revocation concept
The process of invalidating a digital credential or certificate so it can no longer be used.
risk management concept
Risk management is the process of identifying, reducing, and preparing for things that could go wrong.
Roblox product
Roblox is an online gaming platform where users create and play games and buy virtual items.
RogueWinRM tool
A security tool or malware component referenced in reporting that uses Windows Remote Management capabilities.
root concept
The superuser account on Unix and Linux systems that has unlimited control over the entire computer.
also: root-level command execution
root privileges concept
Root privileges are the highest level of control on Unix-like systems, allowing a user or program to change almost anything.
root-level concept
Root-level means having the highest level of control over a device or operating system.
root-level code execution technique
The ability to run commands or programs with the highest level of control on a computer.
Rosstat organization
Rosstat is Russia's federal government agency for official statistics.
Routines product
A Jamf capability for automating recurring device-management tasks.
run code concept
To run code means to make a computer execute instructions written in a programming language.
russia
Russia is a country frequently referenced in cybersecurity stories involving cybercrime groups, espionage, and government activity.
Russia's Supreme Court organization
Russia's Supreme Court is the country's highest court for many legal cases.
Russian government organization
The Russian government is Russia's national governing organization and is often mentioned in cyber and geopolitical reporting.
Russian military organization
The Russian military is Russia's armed forces and may be referenced in security reporting when discussing state-linked activity.
Russian Military Losses concept
Russian military losses are reported casualties and equipment losses suffered by Russia's armed forces.
SaaS concept
SaaS is software delivered over the internet as a subscription or hosted service instead of installed and managed entirely by the customer.
Sabcobel organization
A company associated with refrigeration-system equipment and services.
Sageworks product
Financial software used by lenders to assess business risk and manage lending decisions.
Sageworks Analyst product
A Sageworks software service used by financial institutions to analyze lending and business risk information.
Sageworks API product
A programming interface that lets other software communicate with Sageworks services.
salesforce product
Salesforce is a cloud platform for customer relationship management, sales, service, and business applications.
Salt Typhoon threat-actor
A Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known for targeting telecommunications infrastructure.
sandbox-escape technique
A technique where malware breaks out of a restricted, isolated testing environment to attack the real underlying system.
also: sandbox escape research
Saved passwords concept
Saved passwords are login credentials stored by a browser, app, or password manager for later use.
scams concept
Scams are dishonest schemes designed to trick people into giving money, information, or access.
scanning technique
Scanning is checking computers, networks, or services to find what is reachable and what may be vulnerable.
scans concept
Scans are automated checks that examine software or related data for issues or information.
scheduled-tasks
Scheduled tasks are automated jobs on a computer that attackers can abuse to run malware at specific times or after reboot.
SCL concept
SCL is a spam confidence level score used to help decide how suspicious an email is.
also: spam confidence level
screenshots concept
Images that capture what is currently shown on a computer screen.
search_social.php tool
A PHP script referenced in security reporting.
Secure email gateway product
A secure email gateway is a filter that checks incoming and outgoing email for spam, phishing, malware, and policy violations.
also: SEG
Secure Gateways product
Protected connection points that control and filter traffic between networks or systems.
Security alerts concept
Security alerts are warnings from tools or services that something suspicious or risky may be happening.
Security fixes concept
Security fixes are software updates that repair weaknesses attackers could exploit.
also: fixes, bug fixes, security repairs
Security flaws concept
Weaknesses or mistakes in software or systems that attackers may be able to exploit.
security leaders concept
Security leaders are people responsible for guiding an organization’s cybersecurity strategy and teams.
security measures concept
Security measures are steps or tools used to reduce the chance or impact of security problems.
security operations concept
The function within an organization that continuously monitors, manages, and responds to cybersecurity threats.
Security Operations Centers organization
Security Operations Centers are teams or facilities that monitor an organization’s systems for cyber threats and respond to incidents.
security posture concept
Security posture is the overall strength of an organization's defenses, risks, and readiness to handle cyber threats.
security professionals concept
Security professionals are people whose job is to protect systems, data, and organizations from security threats.
security researchers organization
Security researchers are people who study systems, software, and attacks to find vulnerabilities and improve defenses.
Security Systems concept
Security systems are tools and processes used to protect computers, networks, and information.
security teams concept
Groups of professionals responsible for protecting an organization's information, systems, and networks from cyber threats.
security testing concept
Security testing is checking software, systems, or networks to find weaknesses before attackers can exploit them.
Security Update concept
A software update that fixes vulnerabilities or other security-related problems.
security updates concept
Security updates are software fixes that close vulnerabilities or improve protection against threats.
self-hosted deployments concept
Installations of software that an organization runs and maintains on its own infrastructure rather than using the vendor's hosted service.
Self-hosted instances concept
Self-hosted instances are copies of software that an organization runs on its own servers instead of using a vendor-hosted service.
self-managed deployments concept
Self-managed deployments are software installations that an organization runs and maintains on its own infrastructure.
Selver organization
An Estonian supermarket retail chain.
Semiconductor concept
A semiconductor is a material used to make computer chips and other electronic components.
sensitive data concept
Sensitive data is information that could cause harm if exposed, such as passwords, financial details, or medical records.
sensitive information concept
Sensitive information is data that should be protected because exposing it could harm a person, company, or system.
sensitive patient data concept
Sensitive patient data is medical or personal information about patients that must be protected from unauthorized access.
Sensitive records concept
Sensitive records are stored pieces of information that could harm people or organizations if exposed.
separate infrastructure concept
Separate infrastructure means using distinct servers, networks, or accounts so one system is isolated from another.
Server Wiping technique
A destructive attack technique that deletes or overwrites data on a server to disrupt recovery and operations.
Service Outage concept
A service outage is a period when a system, website, or service is unavailable or not working properly.
service provider organization
A service provider is a company or organization that delivers a service, such as hosting, software, payments, or IT support, to customers.
Session access concept
Session access means the ability to use an active logged-in session, sometimes allowing someone to act as that user without knowing the password.
severity concept
Severity is a rating that describes how serious a security issue is.
SFTP protocol
SFTP is a secure file transfer protocol that uses encryption to move files between computers.
sh tool
sh is a basic Unix command shell used to run scripts and system commands.
Shadowserver organization
Shadowserver is an internet security watchdog group that tracks exposed systems and other security data.
shared infrastructure concept
Shared infrastructure is computing or network equipment used by multiple services, customers, or attackers.
SHELBYC2 malware
A backdoor malware family that gives attackers remote access to an infected computer.
SHELBYLOADER malware
A malware loader used to install or launch other malicious software on a victim's device.
ShelbyLoader V2 malware

shell tool
A shell is a command-line interface that lets a user or program run commands on a computer.
Shell Scripts tool
Text files containing commands that a command-line shell can run automatically.
also: bash script, zip_mails.sh
shinyhunters
ShinyHunters is a cybercrime group known for stealing and selling large databases of user information.
ShinyHunters threat-actor
ShinyHunters is a cybercriminal group known for data theft, extortion, and selling stolen information.
SIEM product
A security tool that gathers and analyzes logs from across an organization in real time to spot suspicious activity.
Sign-In concept
Sign-in is the process of proving your identity to access a computer, account, or online service.
Signed Binary Proxy Execution technique
A technique in which attackers misuse legitimate, digitally signed programs to run commands or malicious code.
signed-in accounts concept
Signed-in accounts are user accounts that are currently logged in to an app, device, or website.
Silent Crow threat-actor
Silent Crow is a pro-Ukrainian hacking group referenced in security reporting.
Silent Train threat-actor
Silent Train is a threat-actor or infrastructure label used in security reporting for covert attacker activity.
Simulations concept
Simulations are practice scenarios that imitate real events so people or systems can test how they would respond.
Single-Label Hostname concept
A hostname with only one name part, such as "server," rather than a public domain name like "server.example.com."

Sirens concept
Loud warning devices used to alert people to emergencies.
situational awareness concept
An understanding of what is happening around an organization, including current threats and risks.
skill concept
A voice-driven application that adds capabilities to a smart assistant like Amazon Alexa, similar to an app on a phone.
slack
Slack is a workplace messaging and collaboration platform.
Slack workspaces product
Slack workspaces are shared online areas where an organization’s members communicate in channels, send messages, and share files.
Smart App Control product
Smart App Control is a Windows security feature that helps block untrusted or potentially malicious apps from running.
SmartScreen product
SmartScreen is a Microsoft security feature that warns users about suspicious downloads, apps, and websites.

Snowflake product
Snowflake is a cloud data platform used to store and analyze data.
SOC organization
SOC stands for security operations center, a team or function that monitors and responds to security issues.
SOC analyst concept
A SOC analyst is a security operations center worker who monitors alerts, investigates suspicious activity, and helps respond to incidents.
social engineering technique
Social engineering is manipulation of people into doing something or sharing information they otherwise would not.
social engineering campaigns technique
Social engineering campaigns are coordinated attempts to trick people into revealing information, clicking links, or taking actions that help an attacker.
Social engineering lures technique
Social engineering lures are tricks or messages designed to persuade people to click, download, or reveal information.
also: context-tailored social engineering lures
social media concept
Social media means online platforms where people share messages, photos, videos, and other content.
Social media accounts concept
Social media accounts are online profiles on platforms like Instagram, X, Facebook, or TikTok that attackers may try to steal or impersonate.
Social Security numbers concept
Social Security numbers are U.S. government identification numbers often targeted by criminals because they can be used for fraud.
Software flaws vulnerability
Software flaws are mistakes or weaknesses in programs that can cause bugs or create security risks.
Software Update concept
A newer version of software that may add improvements or fix problems and security flaws.
software updates concept
Software updates are new versions or fixes released to improve features, repair bugs, or close security holes.
Software Versions concept
Numbered releases of a software product that identify which update or build is installed.
SOHO concept
SOHO means small office/home office, referring to devices and networks used by small businesses or households.
south-korea
South Korea is an East Asian country often referenced in cybersecurity stories involving technology, espionage, or regional threats.
SPAR Colruyt organization
A supermarket business operating SPAR stores associated with the Colruyt Group.
spear-phishing technique
Spear-phishing is a targeted scam message crafted for a specific person or organization to trick them into revealing information or taking an unsafe action.
spearphishing technique
Spearphishing is a targeted scam message sent to a specific person or group to trick them into giving access or information.
spearphishing-link
A spearphishing link is a targeted phishing message that includes a malicious link tailored to a specific person or organization.
also: T1566.002, Phishing: Spearphishing Link
